doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Magazine assignments and turning to children's books
summary: How he found magazine work, travel and social-science stories, and how agent Lynn Nesbit started his successful children's book career.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: They would call you with assignments or would you submit ideas?

It worked both ways. I mean you’re always looking, you’ve got to make sure you’ve got some work. So if they called you great. Hey Jim would you be interested in thus and so. If they didn’t call you you’d be out hustling. Hey Charlie I’m going to be in town on Wednesday I thought I might drop by, whatever, see what you can get. But I never wanted to do that. My father had been in the magazine business, my uncle I mean knew a lot of that magazine business. It wasn’t interesting. I mean I take that back. You did a lot of interesting things. I did a lot of travel eventually, not at the beginning. Eventually I was going to all sorts of places and meeting a lot of people that I wanted to meet. I’ve met a lot of movie stars and all of that, but that goes with the territory. But basically what I was interested in, I was very interested in social sciences and if I knew somebody had done a study on something or other I was interested and I’d cook up a story where I could bring him in. And then I’d get a free ticket to go down to New Orleans and interview the guy at Tulane you know, or whatever. So there was a lot of fun in a lot of that. But the writing itself was not challenging. I could sit down and knock that stuff out in a morning. It was nothing. And so all the time I was also developing some of these other kinds of things, particularly my children’s books which I got into simply because some agent, Lynn Nesbit who went on to become quite a well known agent, Lynn suggested I start doing this. And the children’s books became what certainly is important of what I’ve written, not the jazz stuff. I mean the jazz stuff, that’s fine and it’s good and I’m proud of it, but the children’s stuff, I’ve sold millions of copies of the stuff and not only that I’ve been able to write the so-called prize winning, the quality kind of children’s book that is

difficult and is interesting and is challenging and still make a living from it. And that to me has been the great blessing, that I could write and have reached the point now and have been at this point for some years where I can call my own shots. I write when I want to write and I generally manage to get paid for enough of it so that I can keep going with it.
